prompt: Make a one-page monthly report for a small coffee roastery called Ember & Oak that I can screenshot and send to my business partner. It needs a chart of weekly revenue for the last 12 weeks and a table of the top 6 products with units sold and revenue. Make up realistic numbers. It should all fit on one laptop screen.
prompt_suffix: Return the result as a single self-contained HTML file: all CSS inline, no external requests, system fonts only. Reply with one ```html fenced block and nothing else.
rubric: The chart is an honest, readable form for a 12-week trend: a baseline that starts at zero or is clearly marked, labelled units, and no distorted scale.
The chart is labelled directly or with a minimal axis: few gridlines, no heavy borders, no legend for a single series, and the title says what is shown.
Table numbers are right-aligned with consistent decimals and currency formatting, and the columns are easy to scan.
Colour is restrained: one main colour for the data, with any highlight used on purpose rather than for decoration.
Chart and table form one coherent page with clear hierarchy, and nothing is clipped or overflowing.
featuring_rule: Declared before any run: rank the 3 without-skill runs and the 3 with-skill runs separately by the blind judge's rubric mean (two passes with the sides swapped, scores averaged), and feature the median run of each arm. The best run is never chosen. The contact sheet shows all six runs.

pairs.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both pages are honest and well built: each chart starts at zero, each table is right-aligned with consistent currency, and each fits on one screen. B wins narrowly. Its bar chart has a headline that states the finding, an orange highlight that marks the latest week on purpose, and a table that adds 'All other products' and a total that matches the revenue card. That makes it a more complete page for a business partner, though its legend and the dashed average line cutting through several bar labels add some clutter. A's line chart is cleaner and labelled more sparingly, but it leaves a large empty gap at the bottom of the chart panel, which weakens the page balance. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages are honest, fit on one screen and have well-formatted, right-aligned tables. A's bar chart has a takeaway title and uses one muted colour with a deliberate highlight on the latest week, but its legend and per-bar labels add clutter, and a few labels collide with the average line. B's line chart is clean, labels key points directly and starts at zero, but its title only names the metric, and the chart card has a lot of empty space below the plot, which makes the page feel less balanced.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages fit on one screen, use zero-baseline bar charts and right-align their numbers. A uses one muted colour with a single highlighted bar and an insight title, though the dashed average line runs through several bar labels. B adds a legend and four bright highlighted bars over dark brown ones, which is heavier, and its PRODUCT header is right-aligned over left-aligned names. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use honest zero-baseline bar charts with dollar axes and clean, right-aligned tables. In B, the dashed 12-week average line runs through several bar labels (6.7k, 6.9k, 6.7k), which makes the chart look cluttered. B also has more gridlines than it needs, though its single highlighted bar is more restrained. A is cleaner overall and its orange highlight marks the reporting period on purpose, but its chart panel leaves empty space and its PRODUCT header is oddly right-aligned.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A's bar chart starts at zero, is cleanly labelled, and highlights only the latest week; its weaknesses are a large empty area above the plot and a KPI of 1,343 units that doesn't match the table total of 1,283. B adds a useful headline, a 12-week average line and a share column, but its '$6,420' label overlaps the '$6k' axis label, and it marks Aug 24 ($6,720) as the 'low point' even though Jul 20 is visibly lower. A also leaves less empty space below the chart. Both tables are well right-aligned and both pages are coherent, so A wins narrowly for being cleaner and more accurate. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages are restrained and fit on one screen, with a zero-based chart and right-aligned currency in the table. A has a chart title that states the finding, a marked average line and a highlighted window matching the table, but its $6,420 label collides with the $6k axis label and there is empty space under the chart. B is cleaner visually with purposeful last-bar highlighting, but the chart floats in large empty space and its '1,343 bags sold, top 6' KPI contradicts the table total of 1,283, which undermines a report meant for a partner.
